## Independence

### Definitions

Work on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$.

::: {#def-aap-2-1 name="Independent Events"}

The events $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ are **independent** if, for every nonempty
$I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$,

$$
P\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\right)=\prod_{i\in I}P(A_i).
$$

For two events this reads $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

:::

::: {#def-aap-2-2 name="Independent σ-Fields"}

The sub-$\sigma$-fields $\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F$
are **independent** if

$$
P\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n A_i\right)=\prod_{i=1}^n P(A_i)
\qquad\text{whenever }A_i\in\mathcal F_i.
$$

:::

::: {#def-aap-2-3 name="Independent Random Variables"}

The random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are **independent** if

$$
P(X_1\in B_1,\ldots,X_n\in B_n)=\prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i\in B_i)
\qquad\text{for all }B_1,\ldots,B_n\in\mathcal R.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why No Condition on Subsets" collapse="true"}

Every $\mathcal F_i$ contains $\Omega$, so setting $A_i=\Omega$ (or
$B_i=\mathbb R$) removes index $i$ from both sides. The product rule for all
$n$ therefore implies it for every subfamily, so unlike @def-aap-2-1 no
condition on subsets is needed.

For events this fails: with $A_3=\varnothing$,
$P(A_1\cap A_2\cap A_3)=P(A_1)P(A_2)P(A_3)=0$ holds automatically, even when
$A_1$ and $A_2$ are not independent.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-1 name="Independence and Generated σ-Fields"}

i) If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ are independent.

ii) If $\mathcal G,\mathcal H$ are independent sub-$\sigma$-fields, $X$ is
    $\mathcal G$-measurable, and $Y$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, then $X$ and
    $Y$ are independent.

:::

### Distributions and Expectations

::: {#thm-aap-2-2 name="Joint Distribution of Independent Random Variables"}

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent and $X_i$ has distribution $\mu_i$, then
$(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ has distribution $\mu_1\times\cdots\times\mu_n$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-3 name="Expectations of Functions of Independent Random Variables"}

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent with distributions $\mu$ and $\nu$, and let
$h:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $h\ge0$ or $E|h(X,Y)|<\infty$.
Then

$$
E[h(X,Y)]=\iint_{\mathbb R^2}h(x,y)\,\mu(dx)\,\nu(dy).
$$

In particular, if $f,g\ge0$ or $E|f(X)|,E|g(Y)|<\infty$, then
$E[f(X)g(Y)]=E[f(X)]\,E[g(Y)]$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-4 name="Expectation of a Product of Independent Random Variables"}

If $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent and either all $X_i\ge0$ or all
$E|X_i|<\infty$, then

$$
E\left[\prod_{i=1}^n X_i\right]=\prod_{i=1}^n EX_i.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-5 name="Distribution of the Sum of Independent Random Variables"}

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent with distribution functions $F$ and $G$, then

$$
P(X+Y\le z)=\int_{\mathbb R}F(z-y)\,dG(y)=:(F*G)(z),
$$

the **convolution** of $F$ and $G$. Here $dG$ means integration against the
distribution of $Y$.

:::

## Conditional Expectation

::: {#def-aap-2-7 name="Conditional Expectation"}

Given a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F_0,P)$, a sub-$\sigma$-field
$\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal F_0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable random
variable $X$ with $E|X|<\infty$, the conditional expectation of $X$ given
$\mathcal F$, denoted $E(X\mid\mathcal F)$, is any random variable $Y$ satisfying:

i) $Y$ is $\mathcal F$-measurable.

ii) For all $A\in\mathcal F$,

    $$
    \int_A X\,dP=\int_A Y\,dP.
    $$

Any $Y$ satisfying (i) and (ii) is called a version of $E(X\mid\mathcal F)$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Conditioning on a Random Variable" collapse="true"}

Let $E|X|<\infty$ and $\mathcal F=\sigma(Z)$. Then

$$
Y=E[X\mid\mathcal F]=E[X\mid Z]=g(Z)\quad\text{a.s.}
$$

Here $Y$ is an $\mathcal F$-measurable **random variable**, and $g$ is measurable. Pointwise,

$$
Y(\omega)=g(Z(\omega))\quad\text{for almost every }\omega.
$$

Thus, $Y$ depends only on $Z$; observing $Z=z$ determines its value $g(z)$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Conditional Expectation as Optimal Prediction" collapse="true"}

If $E[X^2]<\infty$, $Y=E[X\mid Z]$ is the best predictor of $X$ based on $Z$ under squared loss:

$$
E[(X-Y)^2]=\min_{h\text{ measurable}}E[(X-h(Z))^2].
$$

In regression, $Z$ contains the input features and $X$ is the target; training with squared loss approximates $E[X\mid Z]$ within the chosen model class.

:::

### Regular Conditional Probabilities

::: {#def-aap-2-8 name="Regular Conditional Distribution"}

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space,
$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\mathcal S)$ a measurable map, and
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-$\sigma$-field. A map
$\mu:\Omega\times\mathcal S\to[0,1]$ is a regular conditional distribution
for $X$ given $\mathcal G$ if:

i) For each $A\in\mathcal S$, $\omega\mapsto\mu(\omega,A)$ is a version of
   $P(X\in A\mid\mathcal G)$.

ii) For almost every $\omega$, $A\mapsto\mu(\omega,A)$ is a probability
    measure on $(S,\mathcal S)$.

When $S=\Omega$ and $X$ is the identity map, $\mu$ is called a regular
conditional probability.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Conditional Distribution from a Joint Density" collapse="true"}

Suppose $X,Y$ have a joint density $f(x,y)>0$. For Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, define

$$
\mu(y,A)=\frac{\displaystyle\int_A f(x,y)\,dx}
{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb R}f(x,y)\,dx}.
$$

Where the denominator is not finite and positive, choose any fixed probability distribution instead.

Then $(\omega,A)\mapsto\mu(Y(\omega),A)$ is a **regular conditional distribution** of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$: $\mu(y,\cdot)$ gives the distribution of $X$ after observing $Y=y$.

:::

## Laws of Large Numbers


### Weak Laws of Large Numbers

::: {#thm-aap-2-7 name="Weak Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables such that

$$
x\,\mathbb{P}(|X_1|>x)\longrightarrow 0
\qquad \text{as } x\to\infty.
$$

Define the partial sum and the truncated mean by

$$
S_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i,
\qquad
\mu_n=\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_1\mathbf{1}_{\{|X_1|\le n\}}\right].
$$

Then

$$
\frac{S_n}{n}-\mu_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}0.
$$

:::
    

### Borel-Cantelli Lemmas

::: {#def-aap-2-9 name="Limit Superior and Limit Inferior of Sets"}

Let $A_n$ be a sequence of subsets of $\Omega$. Define

$$
\limsup A_n=\lim_{m\to\infty}\bigcup_{n=m}^\infty A_n
=\{\omega\text{ that are in infinitely many }A_n\},
$$

where the limit exists since $\bigcup_{n=m}^\infty A_n$ is decreasing in $m$, and

$$
\liminf A_n=\lim_{m\to\infty}\bigcap_{n=m}^\infty A_n
=\{\omega\text{ that are in all but finitely many }A_n\}.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-8 name="Characterization of Almost Sure Convergence"}

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be random variables on a probability space. Then

$$
X_n \xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}} 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathbb P(|X_n|>\epsilon\text{ i.o.})=0
\quad\text{for every }\epsilon>0,
$$

where **i.o.** means *infinitely often*. If $A_n(\epsilon)=\{|X_n|>\epsilon\}$, then

$$
\{|X_n|>\epsilon\text{ i.o.}\}
=\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_n(\epsilon).
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-9 name="Borel-Cantelli Lemma"}

If $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<\infty$, then

$$
\mathbb P(A_n\text{ i.o.})=0.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-10 name="Kolmogorov's Maximal Inequality"}

Suppose $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent with $\mathbb E X_i=0$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(X_i)<\infty$. If $S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n$, then for every
$\epsilon>0$,

$$
\mathbb P\left(\max_{1\le k\le n}|S_k|\ge\epsilon\right)
\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_n)}{\epsilon^2}.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Comparison with Chebyshev's Inequality" collapse="true"}

Under the same hypotheses, Chebyshev's inequality gives only

$$
\mathbb P(|S_n|\ge\epsilon)\le\frac{\operatorname{Var}(S_n)}{\epsilon^2}.
$$

@thm-aap-2-10 gives the same bound for $\displaystyle \max_{1\le k\le n}|S_k|$, which is
at least $|S_n|$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-11 name="Kolmogorov's One-Series Theorem"}

Suppose $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ are independent with $\mathbb E X_n=0$. If

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty\operatorname{Var}(X_n)<\infty,
$$

then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty X_n(\omega)$ converges almost surely.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-2-12 name="Kronecker's Lemma"}

If $a_n\uparrow\infty$ and $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n/a_n$ converges, then

$$
\frac{1}{a_n}\sum_{m=1}^n x_m\to0.
$$

:::

### Strong Law of Large Numbers

::: {#thm-aap-2-13 name="Strong Law of Large Numbers"}

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables with $\mathbb E|X_i|<\infty$.
Let $\mathbb E X_i=\mu$ and $S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n$. Then

$$
\frac{S_n}{n}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mu
\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty.
$$

:::
